entries.meaning: To praise someone or something publicly and enthusiastically. ---
examples: Critics acclaimed the young pianist after her first concert.
Readers still acclaim him as the finest writer of his generation.
Her second novel has been widely acclaimed.
entries.contrast: Most often used in the passive: a widely acclaimed writer.

entries.meaning: To tell someone firmly but not angrily that they have done something wrong. ---
examples: Teachers often admonish students who talk during a test.
The judge admonished him for interrupting.
She has admonished the boys twice about their language.
entries.contrast: Ends in -sh, so the third person adds -es: admonishes.

entries.meaning: To annoy someone, or to make a bad situation worse. ---
examples: His constant humming aggravates everyone in the office.
She aggravated her sister by reading her messages.
He was aggravating the neighbors with loud music all weekend.
entries.contrast: In American English it means both annoy a person and make a problem worse — the context decides which.

entries.meaning: To make people stop being friendly toward you. ---
examples: Try not to alienate the people who can still help you.
His rudeness alienated half the family.
She is alienating the friends who supported her.

entries.meaning: To make someone dislike you or become hostile toward you. ---
examples: Try not to antagonize your brother before the trip.
He antagonized the neighbors by parking in their spot.
She has antagonized everyone on the committee.
entries.contrast: American antagonize; British antagonise.

entries.meaning: To calm an angry person by giving them what they want. ---
examples: He brought flowers to appease his wife.
The apology appeased her for about an hour.
They have been appeasing the angry neighbors all week.

entries.meaning: To keep away from a person or a situation on purpose. ---
examples: She avoids her ex at every party.
He avoided me for a week after the argument.
They have been avoiding each other since the wedding.
entries.contrast: avoid takes the -ing form, never the infinitive: avoid meeting him, not avoid to meet him.

entries.meaning: To keep asking someone for something until they are worn out. ---
examples: Don't badger your sister about the money.
Reporters badgered him with questions for an hour.
She has been badgering me all month to join her book club.

entries.meaning: To say unkind things about someone behind their back (informal). ---
examples: Don't badmouth your coworkers in front of the boss.
He badmouthed his old team in an interview.
She has been badmouthing me to all our friends.

entries.meaning: To exchange light, friendly jokes with someone. ---
examples: The two cousins banter every time they meet.
They bantered about baseball for an hour.
He was bantering with the waitress while we waited.

entries.meaning: To signal someone to come toward you, usually with your hand. ---
examples: The doorman will beckon you when the car arrives.
She beckoned me over with one finger.
He stood at the gate, beckoning to the children.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (beckon the waiter), intransitive (she beckoned to me)

entries.meaning: To make a person or their achievements seem small or unimportant. ---
examples: Don't belittle what she has accomplished.
He belittled his wife in front of the guests.
She felt belittled by his comment about her job.

entries.meaning: To scold someone loudly and at length. ---
examples: Never berate a child in public.
The coach berated the team at halftime.
He has been berating the staff all morning.

entries.meaning: To tell a secret that you were supposed to keep (informal). ---
examples: Don't blab about the surprise party.
Someone blabbed to her mother.
He has been blabbing our news all week.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (blab a secret), intransitive (someone blabbed)
entries.contrast: The single b doubles: blab → blabbed → blabbing.

entries.meaning: To form a close personal connection with someone. ---
examples: New parents often bond with other new parents.
The two men bonded over their love of fishing.
The team has bonded since the coach changed.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the trip bonded the group), intransitive (they bonded quickly)
entries.contrast: bond with someone — the preposition is almost always with.

entries.meaning: To annoy someone, especially by not leaving them alone (informal). ---
examples: Stop bugging me about the car.
His whistling bugged everyone on the bus.
It has bugged me for years that she never called back.
entries.contrast: The single g doubles: bug → bugged → bugging.

entries.meaning: To touch someone gently and lovingly. ---
examples: She caresses his hand whenever he is nervous.
He caressed her cheek and said good night.
She sat caressing the baby's hair until he slept.
entries.contrast: Two s's, and the third person adds -es: caresses.

entries.meaning: To criticize someone sharply for something they have done. ---
examples: Parents sometimes chastise their children in public.
The principal chastised the students for the prank.
He was chastised in the press for his remarks.

entries.meaning: To gently persuade someone to do something they are unwilling to do. ---
examples: It took an hour to coax an apology out of him.
She coaxed her shy brother into dancing.
They were coaxing Grandma to stay another night.
entries.contrast: Ends in -x, so the third person adds -es: coaxes.

entries.meaning: To treat someone too gently and protect them from every difficulty. ---
examples: Don't coddle the kids so much.
His parents coddled him well into his twenties.
She has been coddling her students all semester.

entries.meaning: To live near or with other people without fighting. ---
examples: The two families coexist peacefully on the same street.
For years the groups coexisted without trouble.
They have coexisted in one apartment since March.
entries.contrast: The -x- here sounds like gz: koh-ig-ZIST.

entries.meaning: To accept behavior that most people think is wrong. ---
examples: The school does not condone bullying.
She condoned his rudeness for years.
By saying nothing, he has condoned their behavior.

entries.meaning: To tell someone private things because you trust them. ---
examples: He confides only in his oldest friend.
She confided in her sister about the divorce.
I have never confided that to anyone.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (confide a secret), intransitive (confide in a friend)
entries.contrast: You confide in a person, but you confide a secret to someone.

entries.meaning: To come together in a group in one place. ---
examples: Students congregate in the hallway between classes.
A crowd congregated outside the church.
People were congregating near the entrance.

entries.meaning: To try to win someone's love or support over a period of time. ---
examples: Companies court students at job fairs.
He courted her for two years before proposing.
The candidate is courting younger voters.

entries.meaning: To hold someone close in your arms to show affection. ---
examples: They like to cuddle on the couch and watch movies.
She cuddled the baby until he fell asleep.
The kids were cuddling under one blanket.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (cuddle the baby), intransitive (they cuddled on the couch)

entries.meaning: To have earned something by what you are or what you have done. ---
examples: She deserves a better friend than him.
He deserved that apology and never got it.
They have deserved every bit of their good luck.
entries.contrast: A state verb: say he deserves it, not he is deserving it.

entries.meaning: To consider someone or something beneath your attention. ---
examples: He disdains small talk at parties.
She disdained their offer of help.
They have always disdained people who brag.

entries.meaning: To bring shame on a person or a family. ---
examples: She refused to disgrace her parents' name.
He disgraced the family with his behavior at the wedding.
The former mayor has been disgraced by the scandal.

entries.meaning: To say publicly that you no longer consider someone part of your family. ---
examples: Her father threatened to disown her.
They disowned their son after the trial.
He has been disowned by the whole family.

entries.meaning: To treat someone rudely, as if they did not deserve respect. ---
examples: Don't disrespect your grandmother like that.
He felt she had disrespected him in front of his friends.
You are disrespecting everyone who worked on this.

entries.meaning: To feel that someone cannot be trusted. ---
examples: She distrusts anyone who talks too much.
He distrusted his new neighbors from the start.
Voters have distrusted him since the scandal.

entries.meaning: To leave a person you are with, suddenly and without warning (informal). ---
examples: Don't ditch your friends for a new boyfriend.
She ditched us at the mall and went home.
He has been ditching class to see her.
entries.contrast: Ends in -ch, so the third person adds -es: ditches.

entries.meaning: To control a person or a group, or to take up most of the attention. ---
examples: One family dominates the town's politics.
Her older brother dominated every conversation.
He has been dominating the group since he joined.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (dominate the conversation), intransitive (one voice always dominates)

entries.meaning: To love someone so much that you give them constant attention. ---
examples: Grandparents dote on a first grandchild.
She doted on her little brother.
He has always doted on his wife.
entries.contrast: Always with on or upon: dote on someone.

entries.meaning: To run away with someone in order to marry quietly, without a big wedding. ---
examples: Some couples elope to save money.
They eloped to Las Vegas last spring.
By the time we heard, they had already eloped.

entries.meaning: To meet someone unexpectedly, or to run into a difficulty. ---
examples: You may encounter some resistance from his family.
We encountered an old classmate at the airport.
She has encountered the same rudeness before.

entries.meaning: To make someone liked by other people. ---
examples: Complaining about the food will not endear you to your hosts.
She endeared herself to the neighbors by shoveling their walks.
That habit has not endeared him to his in-laws.
entries.contrast: Almost always endear yourself to someone or endear someone to someone.

entries.meaning: To cause people who were close to become distant from each other. ---
examples: Money can estrange even the closest friends.
The argument estranged him from his brother.
She has been estranged from her father for years.
entries.contrast: Usually in the participle: his estranged wife, estranged from her family.

entries.meaning: To deliberately keep someone out of a group or an activity. ---
examples: Please don't exclude the younger kids.
They excluded him from the group chat.
She has felt excluded ever since the move.
entries.contrast: exclude someone from something — the preposition is from.

entries.meaning: To use a person unfairly for your own benefit. ---
examples: Some employers exploit workers who are new to the country.
He exploited his sister's kindness for years.
She felt exploited by her so-called friends.
entries.contrast: The verb is ik-SPLOYT; the noun exploit (a brave deed) is EK-sployt.

entries.meaning: To treat one person better than others, or to prefer one option. ---
examples: Their mother clearly favors the youngest.
The judges favored the local team.
He has always favored his oldest friends.
entries.contrast: American favor, favored, favoring; British favour, favoured, favouring.

entries.meaning: To carry on a long, bitter quarrel with another person or family. ---
examples: They feud over everything, even parking spots.
The two families feuded for three generations.
The brothers were feuding again at Thanksgiving.

entries.meaning: To behave playfully toward someone to show you find them attractive. ---
examples: He flirts with everyone at the office.
She flirted with him all evening.
They were flirting by the coffee machine.
entries.contrast: flirt with someone — never takes a direct object.

entries.meaning: To trick someone into believing something that is not true. ---
examples: You can't fool your own mother.
He fooled us all with that story about his uncle.
She has been fooling people for years.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (fool your friends), intransitive (stop fooling and sit down)

entries.meaning: To give someone a lot of anxious attention, or to worry aloud about small things. ---
examples: Grandma always fusses over the grandchildren.
He fussed about the seating chart all night.
Stop fussing — the guests won't notice.
entries.contrast: fuss over someone = хлопотать вокруг; fuss about something = ворчать из-за. Third person adds -es: fusses.

entries.meaning: To smile very widely, showing your teeth. ---
examples: She grins every time he tells that joke.
He grinned when he saw her at the door.
They stood there grinning at each other.
entries.contrast: The single n doubles: grin → grinned → grinning.

entries.meaning: To punish a child by not letting them go out with friends. ---
examples: If you lie to me again, I will ground you.
His parents grounded him for two weeks.
She has been grounded since the party.
entries.contrast: This verb is regular — grounded. The identical form ground is also the past of the different verb grind.

entries.meaning: To apologize or beg in a way that shows too much humility. ---
examples: You don't have to grovel — just apologize.
He groveled for a week before she forgave him.
She was still groveling the next morning.
entries.contrast: American groveled, groveling (one l); British grovelled, grovelling.

entries.meaning: To bother someone repeatedly with demands or questions (informal). ---
examples: Quit hassling your sister.
The kids hassled him for ice cream all afternoon.
Security has hassled him twice about his badge.

entries.meaning: To interrupt a speaker or performer with rude shouts. ---
examples: Fans heckle the visiting team every year.
Someone in the back heckled the comedian.
He was heckling the speaker until security came.

entries.meaning: To go along with what someone wants so they will not be upset. ---
examples: Just humor him and listen to the story again.
She humored her grandfather for an hour.
We have been humoring him all evening.
entries.contrast: American humor, humored; British humour, humoured.

entries.meaning: To admire someone so much that you see no faults in them. ---
examples: Kids idolize athletes they have never met.
He idolized his older brother.
She has idolized that singer since middle school.
entries.contrast: American idolize; British idolise.

entries.meaning: To make someone part of a group or an activity. ---
examples: Be sure to include the new kid in the game.
They included us in every family holiday.
She has included her stepson in all the plans.
entries.contrast: include someone in something — the preposition is in.

entries.meaning: To let someone have whatever they want, or to allow yourself a pleasure. ---
examples: She indulges her nephews terribly.
He indulged in a long lunch with old friends.
They have been indulging the baby since day one.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (indulge the children), intransitive (indulge in gossip)
entries.contrast: indulge someone = потакать кому-л.; indulge in something = позволить себе что-л.

entries.meaning: To involve yourself in someone else's affairs when you are not wanted. ---
examples: Her mother interferes in every decision they make.
He interfered once too often and lost a friend.
Work has been interfering with their marriage.
entries.contrast: interfere in someone's business, but interfere with a plan or a relationship.

entries.meaning: To come into a place or a situation where you are not welcome. ---
examples: I don't want to intrude on your evening.
Reporters intruded on the family's grief.
She felt he was intruding into her private life.
entries.contrast: intrude on or intrude upon someone.

entries.meaning: To annoy someone in a small but persistent way. ---
examples: His constant advice irks his brother.
It irked her that no one thanked her.
The noise has irked the neighbors for months.

entries.meaning: To keep a person apart from other people. ---
examples: Don't isolate yourself from your friends.
Shyness isolated him all through high school.
She has been isolating herself since the breakup.

entries.meaning: To shout rude, mocking remarks at someone. ---
examples: Boys on the corner jeer at anyone in a suit.
The crowd jeered when he dropped the ball.
They were jeering at the visiting team all night.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the crowd jeered him), intransitive (they jeered at the referee)

entries.meaning: To say something as a joke, especially to tease someone (informal). ---
examples: Don't kid yourself — she isn't coming back.
He kidded his sister about her new haircut.
I was only kidding, and she knew it.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (kid your brother), intransitive (I'm only kidding)
entries.contrast: The single d doubles: kid → kidded → kidding.

entries.meaning: To interfere in matters that are none of your business. ---
examples: His aunt meddles in everyone's marriage.
She meddled once and lost a friend.
Stop meddling in things that don't concern you.
entries.русский: вмешиваться, лезть не в своё дело
entries.contrast: meddle in someone's affairs. Sounds exactly like the noun medal (медаль).

entries.meaning: To move around at a party talking to many different people. ---
examples: Try to mingle instead of standing by the door.
The host mingled with her guests all evening.
They were mingling near the bar when we arrived.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (mingle the two groups), intransitive (she mingled with the guests)
entries.contrast: mingle with someone — the preposition is with.

entries.meaning: To treat a person cruelly or unfairly. ---
examples: No one should mistreat a guest.
They mistreated the old man for years.
She has been mistreated by everyone she trusted.

entries.meaning: To have doubts about whether someone can be trusted. ---
examples: He mistrusts anyone who is too friendly too fast.
She mistrusted his sudden kindness.
They have mistrusted each other since the argument.
entries.contrast: mistrust and distrust mean nearly the same thing; distrust is the more common of the two in American English.

entries.meaning: To find fault with tiny details that do not matter. ---
examples: He nitpicks everything she cooks.
They nitpicked about the seating chart for an hour.
Stop nitpicking and enjoy the party.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (nitpick every sentence), intransitive (he nitpicks constantly)

entries.meaning: To force someone by duty to do something, or to do a favor they asked for. ---
examples: Family ties oblige us to visit at least twice a year.
She asked for one more song, and the band obliged.
He felt obliged to invite his cousin.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (duty obliges us), intransitive (she asked, and he obliged)
entries.contrast: be obliged to do something = быть обязанным сделать что-л.

entries.meaning: To shut someone out of a group completely. ---
examples: Small towns sometimes ostracize anyone who is different.
The other girls ostracized her after the rumor spread.
No one wants to be ostracized by their own family.
entries.contrast: American ostracize; British ostracise.

entries.meaning: To treat someone with great care and comfort. ---
examples: He pampers his wife on her birthday.
They pampered their guests with breakfast in bed.
She has been pampering her sister all week.

entries.meaning: To raise a child and care for them as a mother or father. ---
examples: They parent very differently from their own parents.
She parented four children on her own.
Parenting two teenagers is exhausting.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (parent a teenager), intransitive (they parent very differently)

entries.meaning: To enjoy yourself at a party, usually late into the night. ---
examples: He parties every weekend.
They partied until three in the morning.
We were partying on the roof when it started raining.
entries.contrast: The -y becomes -ies and -ied (parties, partied), but the -ing form keeps the y: partying.

entries.meaning: To speak to someone as if they were less intelligent than you. ---
examples: Don't patronize me — I have done this longer than you have.
He patronized everyone who asked a simple question.
She felt patronized by her younger colleagues.
entries.contrast: American PAY-truh-nyz; British PAT-ruh-nyz. It also means to be a regular customer of a business.

entries.meaning: To keep annoying someone with requests or questions. ---
examples: Stop pestering your brother.
The kids pestered him for a dog all summer.
She has pestered me about it every day this week.

entries.meaning: To play a trick on someone for fun. ---
examples: They prank each other every April Fools' Day.
He pranked his roommate with a rubber spider.
She has been pranking her coworkers all week.

entries.meaning: To ask about things that are private and none of your business. ---
examples: I don't mean to pry, but are you two still together?
She pried until he told her everything.
He is always prying into other people's business.
entries.contrast: The -y becomes -ies and -ied (pries, pried), but the -ing keeps the y: prying.

entries.meaning: To argue about small, unimportant details. ---
examples: Let's not quibble about ten dollars.
They quibbled over who would pay the check.
The cousins were still quibbling when we left.

entries.meaning: To criticize someone sharply for what they have said or done. ---
examples: No one dared to rebuke the boss.
The coach publicly rebuked his star player.
He has been rebuked twice this month.

entries.meaning: To give back the same feeling or favor that someone gave you. ---
examples: They invited us to dinner, so we should reciprocate.
He loved her, but she never reciprocated.
She has reciprocated every kindness we showed her.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (reciprocate a kindness), intransitive (she never reciprocated)

entries.meaning: To marry again after a divorce or the death of a husband or wife. ---
examples: He says he will never remarry.
She remarried two years after the divorce.
Her mother has remarried twice.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (he remarried his first wife), intransitive (she never remarried)
entries.contrast: The -y becomes -ies and -ied (remarries, remarried), but the -ing keeps the y: remarrying.

entries.meaning: To talk with pleasure about things that happened long ago. ---
examples: They love to reminisce at family dinners.
The old friends reminisced about their college years.
We were reminiscing about our first apartment.
entries.contrast: reminisce about something. The ending -sce sounds like -ss: rem-uh-NIS.

entries.meaning: To tell someone with sadness or disappointment that they have let you down. ---
examples: He has nothing to reproach himself for.
She reproached him for forgetting her birthday.
Her eyes were reproaching me the whole evening.
entries.contrast: reproach someone for something. Ends in -ch, so the third person adds -es: reproaches.

entries.meaning: To come together again after a long separation. ---
examples: The agency helps reunite families.
The sisters reunited after thirty years apart.
They have been reunited at last.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (reunite families), intransitive (the band reunited)

entries.meaning: To greet someone respectfully, or to honor them publicly. ---
examples: He salutes his neighbor with a wave every morning.
The soldiers saluted as the general passed.
The town has saluted her for fifty years of service.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (salute an officer), intransitive (the soldiers saluted)

entries.meaning: To chat in a friendly way with people who may be useful to you (informal). ---
examples: She knows how to schmooze a room full of strangers.
He schmoozed with everyone at the reception.
They were schmoozing with donors until midnight.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (schmooze the donors), intransitive (he schmoozed all night)

entries.meaning: To reject or look down on someone with open contempt. ---
examples: They scorn anyone who leaves the neighborhood.
She scorned his apology and walked away.
He has been scorned by his old friends ever since.

entries.meaning: To persuade someone into a romantic relationship, or into doing something unwise. ---
examples: He tried to seduce her with expensive gifts.
The idea of easy money seduced them both.
He was seducing half the town, or so the rumor went.

entries.meaning: To deliberately keep away from a person or from company. ---
examples: She shuns parties and big crowds.
The whole village shunned him after the trial.
They have been shunned by their relatives for years.
entries.contrast: The single n doubles: shun → shunned → shunning.

entries.meaning: To tell someone in authority what another person did wrong (informal). ---
examples: Don't snitch on your own brother.
Someone snitched on us to the principal.
He has been snitching to the boss all year.
entries.contrast: snitch on someone. Ends in -ch, so the third person adds -es: snitches.

entries.meaning: To smile or speak in a way that shows contempt for someone. ---
examples: They sneer at anyone who tries hard.
He sneered at her homemade dress.
She was sneering the whole time I spoke.
entries.contrast: sneer at someone — it takes no direct object.

entries.meaning: To look secretly into someone's private things. ---
examples: Don't snoop around in my room.
She snooped through his phone while he slept.
He has been snooping on the neighbors again.

entries.meaning: To ignore someone on purpose in a way that insults them. ---
examples: Don't snub your cousins just because they came late.
She snubbed him in front of everyone at the party.
He felt snubbed when they left him off the list.
entries.contrast: The single b doubles: snub → snubbed → snubbing.

entries.meaning: To settle close against someone for warmth and comfort. ---
examples: They like to snuggle under one blanket.
The children snuggled against their mother.
The puppy was snuggling into his lap.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (snuggle the baby close), intransitive (they snuggled under a blanket)

entries.meaning: To quarrel noisily over something unimportant. ---
examples: Brothers squabble; that is normal.
The kids squabbled over the last piece of cake.
They were squabbling about money again.

entries.meaning: To tell a parent or teacher what another child did wrong. ---
examples: Nobody likes a kid who tattles.
He tattled on his sister for staying up late.
She was tattling to the teacher every single day.
entries.contrast: tattle on someone — the preposition is on.

entries.meaning: To make someone want to do something, especially something they should not do. ---
examples: Don't tempt him with another drink.
The offer tempted her to leave the city.
I have been tempted to call her all week.

entries.meaning: To worry someone, or to bother them with a request. ---
examples: Sorry to trouble you so late.
The news troubled the whole family.
Something has been troubling her for weeks.

entries.meaning: To remove someone from your list of friends on a social network. ---
examples: Don't unfriend your own cousin over politics.
She unfriended him the day after the argument.
He has unfriended half his old classmates.

entries.meaning: To move your hand in the air to greet someone or say goodbye. ---
examples: Wave goodbye to Grandma.
She waved to us from the train window.
He was waving his arms to get our attention.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (wave your hand), intransitive (she waved from the car)
entries.contrast: The silent -e drops before -ing: wave → waving. You wave to or wave at a person.

entries.meaning: To try to win someone's love, support, or business. ---
examples: Candidates woo voters with easy promises.
He wooed her with letters for a year.
The company has been wooing her since March.
entries.contrast: Both o's stay in every form: woo → wooed → wooing.

entries.meaning: To love and admire someone so deeply that you treat them as perfect.
examples: She worships her older sister.
He worshiped his father when he was a boy.
They have worshiped at the same church for years.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (worship a hero), intransitive (they worship on Sunday)
entries.contrast: American worshiped, worshiping (one p); British worshipped, worshipping.
